title: Two-stage Miller-compensated OTA
topology: A two-stage operational amplifier: a first stage (typically a five-transistor or cascode differential pair) that provides most of the DC gain and sets the input-referred noise and offset, followed by a second common-source gain stage that supplies additional gain and drives the output load. A Miller (pole-splitting) compensation capacitor connects the second stage's output back to its input (the first stage's output node), splitting the amplifier's two dominant poles far apart and trading loop bandwidth for closed-loop stability. Because the compensation capacitor also creates a low-impedance feedforward path through the second-stage transistor, a nulling resistor (or a common-gate/source-follower buffer) is typically placed in series with the compensation capacitor to cancel, or push out, the right-half-plane zero that path introduces.
spec_class: high-gain, wide-output-swing op-amp core for feedback amplifiers driving resistive or large capacitive loads (LDO error amplifiers, filter integrators, output buffers) where a single-stage OTA's limited DC gain or output swing is insufficient

pdk_portability.notes: Pole-splitting Miller compensation and the RHP-zero-cancellation techniques (nulling resistor, or a common-gate/source-follower buffer in the compensation path) are fully portable to any PDK; the specific compensation-capacitor value, nulling-resistor value, and resulting phase margin are sky130-specific because they depend on the first stage's output resistance, the second stage's transconductance, and sky130's parasitic capacitances, so the compensation network must be re-simulated against sky130 device and interconnect models rather than simply re-scaled from another process's design.

sizing_approach: Size the first-stage differential pair and its load for the target input-referred noise, offset, and first-stage gain using a gm/ID design point; size the second stage's common-source device's transconductance so the amplifier's second (non-dominant) pole sits at least roughly 2.2x beyond the desired closed-loop unity-gain bandwidth, using the pole-splitting relation in which the compensation capacitor times the second stage's gm sets the non-dominant pole location; choose the compensation capacitor as the smallest value that places the dominant pole (set by the first stage's output resistance and the Miller-multiplied capacitance) so the loop's unity-gain frequency lands comfortably below the non-dominant pole; add a nulling resistor (or a unity-gain buffer) in series with the compensation capacitor, sized to cancel the RHP zero (nulling resistance approximately 1/gm of the second stage) rather than letting the zero erode phase margin; size the second stage's bias current for the required load-driving slew rate, whichever of I_second-stage/C_compensation or I_second-stage/C_load dominates.
layout_idioms: first-stage differential pair in common-centroid layout, on its own symmetry axis, kept separate from the single-ended second stage to avoid coupling asymmetric loading into the matched pair

Miller compensation capacitor placed close to the second-stage output/input nodes it bridges, implemented as a PDK metal-insulator-metal or poly capacitor and guard-ringed to minimize parasitic coupling into the sensitive first-stage output node

nulling resistor, when implemented as a poly or diffusion resistor rather than a triode-region MOS device, laid out as a matched unit-resistor element in series with the compensation capacitor and routed away from noisy digital circuitry

second-stage output device sized with adequate multi-finger width for the required load-driving current, with substrate/well contacts placed close to the device to limit self-heating and latch-up risk at higher output currents

source.citation: P. R. Gray and R. G. Meyer, "MOS operational amplifier design-a tutorial overview," IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits, vol. 17, no. 6, pp. 969-982, Dec. 1982.
source.license_or_openness: Peer-reviewed IEEE journal paper cited here for its two-stage Miller-compensated op-amp topology and pole-splitting/RHP-zero-cancellation methodology only (no figures or text reproduced), per the KB's open-sources sourcing rule (case 2, peer-reviewed paywalled literature cited for restated methodology only, in kb/SOURCING.md). This is a foundational, widely-cited tutorial establishing Miller pole-splitting compensation as the standard technique for two-stage CMOS op amps.

notes: The classic, most general-purpose op-amp topology when a single stage's DC gain is insufficient; the trade-off versus a folded-cascode OTA is higher achievable DC gain and output swing at the cost of a slower-settling, more compensation-sensitive loop (extra non-dominant pole and RHP zero to manage). sky130's comparatively modest intrinsic device gain (gm*ro) at minimum length makes the two-stage approach attractive whenever a single stage's gain is not enough, provided the design budgets area and simulation effort for corner/temperature verification of the compensation network's phase margin.
